lesson.title: The Citric Acid Cycle: Spinning Carbon Skeletons to Harvest Electrons
lesson.summary: The Krebs cycle is a closed loop of eight enzymatic reactions that fully oxidizes the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA, harvesting its electrons as NADH and FADH2 while regenerating the starting molecule to run again.
lesson.body:
The Krebs cycle, also called the citric acid cycle or the TCA cycle, is where the two-carbon acetyl group carried by acetyl-CoA finally gets completely dismantled. It takes place in the mitochondrial matrix and runs as a closed loop rather than a straight pathway: each turn regenerates the same starting molecule, oxaloacetate, so the cycle can accept another acetyl-CoA and run again indefinitely as long as fuel and oxidized electron carriers are available.

The cycle opens when citrate synthase combines acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form the six-carbon molecule citrate, essentially the reverse energetic direction of what you would expect, made favorable by the energy stored in acetyl-CoA's thioester bond described in the previous section. From there, a sequence of enzymes reshapes citrate through isocitrate, alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, succinate, fumarate, and malate, before finally regenerating oxaloacetate to close the loop. Two of those steps, the conversions to alpha-ketoglutarate and to succinyl-CoA, are oxidative decarboxylations: each releases a carbon as CO2 and reduces an NAD+ to NADH, the same redox chemistry that has been the throughline since glycolysis.

Tallying one single turn of the cycle, which processes one acetyl-CoA, the direct products are 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 ATP or GTP through substrate-level phosphorylation at the succinyl-CoA synthetase step, and 2 CO2. The FADH2 comes from the succinate dehydrogenase step, an enzyme worth remembering because it is physically embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and doubles as Complex II of the electron transport chain, a direct structural link between the Krebs cycle and the next stage of respiration. Because each glucose molecule yields two acetyl-CoA molecules through glycolysis and pyruvate oxidation, the Krebs cycle turns twice per glucose, doubling every one of those numbers: 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 2 ATP or GTP, and 4 CO2 total.

It is worth pausing on where the carbon actually goes. Every carbon atom that entered the cycle as part of glucose eventually leaves as CO2, which is why exhaled carbon dioxide is a direct byproduct of cellular respiration rather than a strange side effect. The oxygen atoms used to build those CO2 molecules come from water and from the carboxyl groups already present in the intermediates, not from molecular oxygen, which is reserved for the very end of the electron transport chain.

None of the ATP made from the Krebs cycle's NADH and FADH2 has actually been produced yet at this point. Those electron carriers are, in a real sense, IOUs: the enzymes have captured high-energy electrons, but converting that potential into ATP requires delivering the electrons to the electron transport chain, where oxidative phosphorylation will finally cash them in. The Krebs cycle's real contribution to ATP yield, then, is mostly indirect, funneling ten NADH and two FADH2 per glucose, once glycolysis and pyruvate oxidation are included, toward the membrane-based machinery covered next.
